articles.title: Benson High Chemical Attack Case Includes References to Online 764 Network
articles.description: FBI Materials in Benson High School Case Included References to 764
articles.content: A 15-year-old accused of mixing toxic chemicals inside Benson Polytechnic High School in Portland now faces attempted-murder and domestic-terrorism charges, and prosecutors say FBI materials tied to the case contain extensive references to a violent online network known as 764. The Sept. 8 incident sent several students and staff members for medical care, and it has since become a flashpoint in a broader reckoning over how these so-called gore groups recruit and manipulate children online. At an October hearing, prosecutors said the FBI was reviewing computers, hard drives and other materials that included extensive references to 764, according to KPTV. The Portland Police Bureau said in a statement that the teen had been criminally charged with crimes including multiple counts of attempted murder and domestic terrorism following the September incident, according to the Portland Police Bureau. Reports on the exact charges have varied slightly. KPTV described the charges as attempted murder and domestic terrorism tied to the Sept. 8 incident, while a separate report from KATU said the teen faces 19 charges total, including 12 counts of attempted murder or attempted aggravated murder along with domestic-terrorism counts. What Investigators Say About 764 U.S. Attorney Scott Bradford has described 764 not as a formal organization but as something more fluid and harder to pin down. “It is a network, but it’s decentralized, and they’re loosely affiliated,” Bradford said, per the same KPTV report. That looseness is part of what makes the group difficult for investigators to track, since cells can form, splinter and rebrand without any central command. The scale of the FBI’s nationwide effort is murky in the public record. OregonLive reported in November 2026 that the FBI was investigating more than 350 people nationwide, as detailed by Oregonlive. KATU attributed a November 2025 figure of more than 350 investigations to ABC News. KATU reported that in a separate update in May 2026, the FBI said more than 450 people were under investigation for links to violent online networks. The November figure counted investigations, while the May figure counted people under investigation. A Pattern Beyond Portland The Department of Homeland Security has warned that these networks can use threats, peer pressure and blackmail to push children toward self-harm or violence, a dynamic federal officials say has accelerated sharply. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s CyberTipline received more than 1,300 reports related to violent online groups in 2024, an increase of more than 200% from 2023, per the KPTV report. Oregon has seen this pattern before. In June 2025, authorities announced the arrest of a St. Helens teenager accused of planning a shooting and bombing at Three Rivers Mall in Kelso, Washington, after the FBI said investigators had found the teenager discussing an attack in an online chat with members of 764. That case ultimately did not end with the most serious charges intact — prosecutors dropped the attempted-murder and attempted-assault counts, and the teenager instead admitted to two counts of disorderly conduct and two counts of unlawful possession of a weapon, the KPTV report notes. Cases Stretching Across North America Similar prosecutions tied to the network have surfaced well outside Oregon. A 17-year-old from Maine with ties to 764 was sentenced to prison for sexually exploiting children, in a case the FBI’s Boston field office said marks the first time a juvenile has been charged in federal court with crimes carried out as part of online nihilistic groups connected to the 764 network, according to NBC News. North of the border, the RCMP charged a 17-year-old in Lethbridge, Alberta, on Sept. 28 with multiple offences, saying the teen’s online activity was consistent with the designated terrorist group 764, as reported by CBC. At the federal level, the Justice Department has also pursued the network’s alleged leadership. The department said Prasan Nepal, known online as “Trippy,” pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit sexual exploitation of a child, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. Together, the cases illustrate a sprawling, cross-border investigative effort — one in which the Benson High School case remains an active and unresolved piece.
creator: emily nguyen
articles.ai_summary: Prosecutors say FBI materials in the case include references to a network known as 764. The Portland teen faces 19 charges, including attempted murder and terrorism, police say. The Sept. 8 incident sent students and staff to medical care after the chemicals were mixed in Benson Polytechnic High School. The scale of FBI’s nationwide effort to investigate violent online networks is murky in public record. In November 2026, the FBI said more than 350 people were being investigated for links to 764 networks.

articles.title: Rewilding Portugal recebe 30 mil euros para preparar regresso do castor
articles.description: O financiamento permitirá recuperar três ribeiras, remover espécies vegetais invasoras, plantar 5.000 árvores autóctones e construir duas pequenas estruturas inspiradas nos diques dos castores, destinadas a favorecer a retenção de água e a recuperação dos ecossistemas.
articles.content: Rewilding Portugal recebe 30 mil euros para preparar regresso do castor O financiamento permitirá recuperar três ribeiras, remover espécies vegetais invasoras, plantar 5.000 árvores autóctones e construir duas pequenas estruturas inspiradas nos diques dos castores, destinadas a favorecer a retenção de água e a recuperação dos ecossistemas. A beaver is swimming along a French river in the Dauphiné Alps A associação de conservação da natureza Rewilding Portugal recebeu 30 mil euros para recuperar três ribeiras no Douro Internacional e criar condições para o regresso natural do castor-europeu, após vencer uma votação pública internacional, foi hoje anunciado. Em comunicado, a associação diz que o projeto português foi um dos dois selecionados entre dez candidaturas finalistas numa votação promovida pela European Outdoor Conservation Association (EOCA), que decorreu entre 5 e 17 de novembro, tendo o resultado sido anunciado na terça-feira, dia 24. O financiamento permitirá recuperar três ribeiras, remover espécies vegetais invasoras, plantar 5.000 árvores autóctones e construir duas pequenas estruturas inspiradas nos diques dos castores, destinadas a favorecer a retenção de água e a recuperação dos ecossistemas. A iniciativa, denominada “The Beaver’s Return: Preparing Rivers for Their Expansion, Portugal” pretende preparar os habitats ribeirinhos para a expansão natural de uma espécie que desapareceu de Portugal há vários séculos. A organização esclarece que o projeto não prevê a introdução ou libertação de castores em território nacional, mas a criação de condições ecológicas favoráveis à sua chegada e expansão natural. O castor-europeu encontra-se em expansão natural na Península Ibérica, com registos da sua presença em zonas próximas da fronteira portuguesa, na região do Douro Internacional, segundo a Rewilding Portugal. A espécie, conhecida pela construção de diques, contribui para a retenção de água, a criação de zonas húmidas e o aumento da biodiversidade, podendo também reforçar a resiliência dos territórios perante fenómenos climáticos extremos, como secas e cheias. O outro projeto vencedor, promovido pela organização Wild Care Nepal, no Nepal, receberá igualmente 30 mil euros para recuperar 100 hectares de zonas húmidas na Reserva de Vida Selvagem de Koshi Tappu e contribuir para a conservação do gato-pescador, um felino selvagem nativo do Sul e Sudeste Asiático. A iniciativa abrange ainda as comunidades piscatórias indígenas, apostando na capacitação de guias locais e no incentivo a alojamentos turísticos geridos por mulheres. No total, os dois projetos selecionados pela votação da EOCA vão receber 60 mil euros para ações de conservação e restauro da natureza.
creator: maria teixeira alves

articles.title: Sri Lanka ‘A’ come up against destructive Sooryavanshi
articles.description: Unbeaten Sri Lanka ‘A’, led by Pavan Rathnayake, will face their first real test when they front up against India ‘A’ in the first semi-final of the Asia Cup Rising Stars 50-over tournament in Doha today.
articles.content: - Take on India ‘A’ in first semi-final today Unbeaten Sri Lanka ‘A’, led by Pavan Rathnayake, will face their first real test when they front up against India ‘A’ in the first semi-final of the Asia Cup Rising Stars 50-over tournament in Doha today. The challenge for the Sri Lanka ‘A’ bowlers is to get the wicket of destructive opener Vaibhav Sooryavanshi early, because he can take the game away from the opposition on his own, as he showed two days ago by smashing the fastest double century in List A cricket, off 53 balls, against UAE. India ‘A’s batting is not all about Sooryavanshi, although he has grabbed the headlines with his extraordinary batting. They have a strong line-up that will test the Lankan ‘A’ bowlers, who have been pretty good so far, dismissing Afghanistan ‘A’ for 139 and Bangladesh ‘A’ for 145. Only against Hong Kong did they come up against strong opposition, conceding 260, but Sri Lanka ‘A’ still managed to win that game by 24 runs. In Captain Tilak Varma and Kumar Kushagra, India ‘A’ have two batters who have scored centuries in the tournament. Abhishek Sharma and Shahbaz Ahmed have also each crossed the fifty-run mark once. Sri Lanka ‘A’s bowling has relied mostly on spin, with Wanuja Sahan, Ravindra Fernando, Vijayakanth Viyaskanth, Chamika Heenatigala and Nipun Dananjaya playing a big role in their victories, supported by the left-arm seam of Dulaj Samuditha. India ‘A’s attack is based mainly on seam, with Prince Yadav, Harshit Rana and Arshad Khan their key wicket-takers. Sri Lanka ‘A’s batting has been tested only once. Against Afghanistan ‘A’ they batted first and ran up 284-9, but in their other two group games they were chasing small totals and were never properly stretched. Opener Lasith Croospulle, one-drop batter Nishan Madushka, skipper Pavan Rathnayake and Janith Liyanage have been the main contributors to the Lankan ‘A’ totals, with Croospulle’s 75 against Hong Kong the highest score. Opener Sineth Jayawardena needs to curb his early aggression and not try to hit every ball he receives out of the park. Once set, he can go after the bowling. This is not a 20-over game but a 50-over one, and there is plenty of time to play yourself in before unleashing your full repertoire of strokes. India ‘A’ suffered one loss on their way to the semi-finals, against arch rivals Pakistan ‘A’, but wins over Nepal and UAE secured them a place in the last four. Pakistan ‘A’ are the only other team to remain unbeaten in the tournament, finishing top of Group B with three wins. They play Bangladesh ‘A’ in the second semi-final on Friday. The final is scheduled for Sunday. (ST)

India ‘a’ have a strong batting line-up which will test the Lankan bowlers. Sri Lankan 'A's bowling has relied on spinners, with Wanuja Sahan and Ravindra Fernando among the bowlers playing a big part in Sri Lanka's victories so far. India have two batsmen who have scored hundreds in the tournament.

articles.title: India A vs Sri Lanka A live streaming: When and where to watch Asia Cup Rising Stars 2026 semi-final
articles.description: In a thrilling showdown, India A is set to face Sri Lanka A in the first semi-final of the ACC Men's Asia Cup Rising Stars on November 26 in Doha. Both squads are eager for victory, aiming for a spot in the grand final. Fans can catch the live action on the Sony Sports Network and the Sony LIV app.
articles.content: India A will face an unbeaten Sri Lanka A in the first semi-final of the ACC Men's Asia Cup Rising Stars 2026 in Doha on Thursday, November 26. With a place in the final at stake, Tilak Varma and his team will be aiming to overcome a formidable Sri Lankan side and continue their title pursuit. India A bounced back from their defeat against Pakistan A with a dominant seven-wicket victory over the UAE in their final group-stage fixture. The match witnessed a sensational batting display from 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, who smashed a record-breaking 204 off just 53 deliveries to help India chase down 250 in only 14.2 overs. Sri Lanka A, meanwhile, have been the most consistent team in the competition. They topped Group A with three consecutive victories, defeating Afghanistan A, Hong Kong and Bangladesh A to enter the semi-final unbeaten. India A vs Sri Lanka A: Match Preview India A finished second in Group B with two wins from three matches. They began their campaign with a commanding 306-run victory over Nepal before suffering a 48-run defeat against Pakistan A. They bounced back against the UAE, chasing down 250 with seven wickets in hand. Sri Lanka A, led by Pavan Rathnayake, have enjoyed an unbeaten run in the group stage. Nishan Madushka has been their leading run-scorer with 145 runs, while Wanuja Sahan has claimed seven wickets. The Sri Lankan bowling attack will look to challenge India's explosive batting line-up, particularly Sooryavanshi, who will enter the knockout fixture after his record-breaking double century India A vs Sri Lanka A Live Streaming: When And Where To Watch? Cricket fans in India can watch the India A vs Sri Lanka A semi-final live on television and digital platforms. Live TV Broadcast: Sony Sports Network Live Streaming: Sony LIV app and website TV Channels: Sony Sports 1, Sony Sports 2, Sony Sports 3 (Hindi), Sony Sports 4 (Tamil and Telugu) Match Start Time: 3:30 PM IST Toss Time: 3:00 PM IST Squads: India A Squad: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Abhishek Sharma, Prabhsimran Singh, Tilak Varma(c), Kumar Kushagra(w), Rinku Singh, Suryansh Shedge, Shahbaz Ahmed, Harsh Dubey, Harshit Rana, Arshad Khan, Ayush Badoni, Tanush Kotian, Prince Yadav, Vipraj Nigam Sri Lanka A Squad: Lasith Croospulle, Sineth Jayawardena, Nishan Madushka(w), Pavan Rathnayake(c), Nipun Dhananjaya, Janith Liyanage, Wanuja Sahan, Lahiru Samarakoon, Ravindu Fernando, Dulaj Samuditha, Vijayakanth Viyaskanth, Garuka Sanketh, Duvindu Ranatunga, Sharujan Shanmuganathan, Chamika Heenatigala

articles.title: Ancient Killer Is Rapidly Gaining Resistance to Antibiotics, Warns Study
articles.description: A deadly threat. ScienceAlert stories are written, fact-checked, and edited by humans, never generated by AI. Don't miss a story, subscribe here.
articles.content: An ancient killer has plagued humans for millennia. Although it's rarely considered a threat in developed countries today, it seems this long-term villain is still very much a danger in our modern world. Research published in 2022 revealed the bacterium that causes typhoid fever is evolving extensive drug resistance and is rapidly replacing strains that aren't resistant. Currently, antibiotics are the only effective treatment for typhoid, caused by the bacterium Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (S. Typhi). Yet over the past three decades, the bacterium's resistance to oral antibiotics has been growing and spreading. In their study, scientists from multiple countries sequenced the genomes of 3,489 S. Typhi strains contracted from 2014 to 2019 in Nepal, Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India, and found a rise in extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Typhi. Watch the video below for a summary of the study: XDR Typhi is not only impervious to frontline antibiotics, like ampicillin, chloramphenicol, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, but it is also growing resistant to newer antibiotics, like fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins. Even worse, these strains are spreading globally at a rapid rate. While most XDR Typhi cases stem from South Asia, researchers have identified nearly 200 instances of international spread since 1990. Most strains have been exported to Southeast Asia, as well as East and Southern Africa, but typhoid superbugs have also been found in the UK, the US, and Canada. "The speed at which highly resistant strains of S. Typhi have emerged and spread in recent years is a real cause for concern, and highlights the need to urgently expand prevention measures, particularly in countries at greatest risk," said Stanford University infectious disease researcher Jason Andrews when the results were published. Scientists have been warning about drug-resistant typhoid for years now. In 2016, the first XDR typhoid strain was identified in Pakistan. By 2019, it had become the dominant genotype in the nation. Historically, most drug-resistant typhoid strains have been treated with third-generation antimicrobials, such as quinolones, cephalosporins, and macrolides. But by the early 21st century, mutations that confer resistance to quinolones accounted for more than 85 percent of all cases in Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Nepal, and Singapore. At the same time, cephalosporin resistance was also taking over. Today, only one oral antibiotic is left: the macrolide, azithromycin. And this medicine might not work for much longer. The 2022 study found that mutations that confer resistance to azithromycin are now also spreading, "threatening the efficacy of all oral antimicrobials for typhoid treatment". While these mutations have not yet been adopted by XDR S Typhi, if they are, we are in serious trouble. If untreated, up to 20 percent of typhoid cases can be fatal, and in 2024, there were over 13 million cases of typhoid reported. Future outbreaks can be prevented to some extent with typhoid conjugate vaccines, but if access to these shots is not expanded globally, the world could soon have another health crisis on its hands. "The recent emergence of XDR and azithromycin-resistant S. Typhi creates greater urgency for rapidly expanding prevention measures, including use of typhoid conjugate vaccines in typhoid-endemic countries," the authors write. "Such measures are needed in countries where antimicrobial resistance prevalence among S. Typhi isolates is currently high, but given the propensity for international spread, should not be restricted to such settings." South Asia might be the main hub for typhoid fever, accounting for 70 percent of all cases, but if COVID-19 taught us anything, it is that disease variants in our modern, globalized world are easily spread. To prevent that from happening, health experts argue nations must expand access to typhoid vaccines and invest in new antibiotic research. A 2021 study in India, for instance, estimated that if children are vaccinated against typhoid in urban areas, it could prevent up to 36 percent of typhoid cases and deaths. Pakistan is leading the way on this front. It was the first nation in the world to offer routine immunization for typhoid. A small number of countries have now followed suit or are "planning or considering introduction". The World Health Organization has prequalified four typhoid conjugate vaccines as of April 2025, according to the CDC, which states, "these vaccines are being introduced into childhood immunization programs in typhoid-endemic countries." Antibiotic resistance is one of the world's leading causes of death, claiming the lives of more people than HIV/AIDS or malaria. Where available, vaccines are among the best tools we have to prevent future catastrophes. We don't have time to waste. The study was published in The Lancet Microbe.
